hints: Remember each peak in a carbon-13 NMR spectrum represents one unique carbon environment, so look for a plane of symmetry that makes carbons equivalent.
Compare the symmetry of F, with two identical para substituents, to G, where all three substituents are different.
walkthrough:
Link peaks to symmetry**
Think of carbon-13 NMR very simply. If two carbons are in exactly the same environment, they give one shared peak. So you are hunting for symmetry that pairs carbons up.

Count for F**
Look at F, $\text{HO}_2\text{C-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$. The two $\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$ groups are identical and para to each other. That gives high symmetry. The two carbonyl carbons are equivalent (1 environment). In the ring, the two carbons attached to $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ are equivalent, the two pairs of CH carbons pair up into two more environments. Total = $1 + 3 = 4$? Wait, check carefully. The ring has: C attached to CO2H (x2 equivalent), ortho CH (x2 equivalent), meta CH (x2 equivalent). Actually that would be 3 ring environments plus 1 carbonyl = 4. But the two types of ring CH carbons in a para disubstituted ring with identical groups are equivalent by symmetry, so ortho and meta pairs merge? Let's redraw mentally. For 1,4 identical substitution, there are only 2 ring carbon types: C-C=O (x2) and C-H (x4). All four C-H carbons are equivalent. So $1$ (carbonyl) $+ 1$ (C-C=O) $+ 1$ (C-H) $= 3$ peaks.

Count for G**
Now look at G, $\text{H}_2\text{N-C}_6\text{H}_3\text{(NH}_2\text{)(OH)}$. The three substituents ($\text{NH}_2$, $\text{NH}_2$, $\text{OH}$) are not all the same and are in 1,3,4 positions. There is no symmetry plane that swaps any carbons. All six ring carbons are in different environments, so you see 6 peaks.

Final answer: F: 3 peaks
G: 6 peaks

hints: Recall that a dicarboxylic acid plus a diamine join by condensation, losing water to form $\text{-CO-NH-}$ links.
Join one $\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$ end of F to one $\text{-NH}_2$ end of G, then repeat at the other ends, keeping the $\text{OH}$ group untouched on the ring.
walkthrough:
Spot the reacting groups**
You have $\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$ on F and $\text{-NH}_2$ on G. When acid meets amine under condensation conditions, $\text{-OH}$ from the acid and $\text{-H}$ from the amine leave as $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, leaving $\text{-C(=O)-NH-}$. That is your amide bond and it must be drawn out in full, showing $\text{C=O}$ and $\text{N-H}$.

Build one repeat unit**
Take the central benzene from F with its two carbonyl carbons, then link each $\text{C=O}$ to an $\text{NH}$ from one molecule of G. So the sequence is: continuation bond, $\text{C(=O)}$, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_4$, $\text{C(=O)}$, $\text{NH}$, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_3\text{(OH)}$, $\text{NH}$, continuation bond. The phenolic $\text{OH}$ on G does not react, it stays as a side group on the ring.

Show polymer correctly**
Draw only one combined unit from F plus G, with a short bond sticking out of each end to show it continues. Do not draw extra brackets with n if you already show continuation bonds, and do not lose the $\text{OH}$.

Final answer: Repeat unit: $\text{-CO-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-CO-NH-C}_6\text{H}_3\text{(OH)-NH-}$ with both amide groups shown displayed as $\text{-C(=O)-NH-}$ and with continuation bonds at each end. $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ eliminated. Only one repeat unit shown.

hints: Picture ethene, $\text{CH}_2\text{=CH}_2$, which contains one sigma bond plus one pi bond between the carbons.
Think about what remains in poly(ethene), $\text{-[CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{]-}_n$, where all carbons are joined by single bonds only.
walkthrough:
See what breaks in ethene**
Each ethene has a $\text{C=C}$ double bond, made of one strong sigma bond and one weaker pi bond. To polymerise, the pi part opens up to give two free valencies, but the sigma bond between those two carbons never breaks. So across many monomers, only pi bonds are broken.

See what forms in the chain**
Those opened valencies join to the next monomer to make new $\text{C-C}$ single bonds along the backbone. A single bond is a sigma bond. No new pi bonds are made. So only sigma bonds are formed.

Final answer: bonds broken: pi-bonds only (tick)
bonds formed: sigma-bonds only (tick)

hints: For addition polymerisation, turn each $\text{C=C}$ into a $\text{C-C}$ single bond and attach the side groups ($\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5$) to alternate backbone carbons.
Join one propene unit, $\text{-CH}_2\text{-CH(CH}_3\text{)-}$, directly to one phenylethene unit, $\text{-CH}_2\text{-CH(C}_6\text{H}_5\text{)-}$, with continuation bonds at both ends.
walkthrough:
Convert each monomer**
Write propene as $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CH}_2$. On polymerising it becomes $\text{-CH}_2\text{-CH(CH}_3\text{)-}$. Do the same for phenylethene, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH=CH}_2$, which becomes $\text{-CH}_2\text{-CH(C}_6\text{H}_5\text{)-}$. The double bond is gone, the substituent stays on one carbon.

Link them as a copolymer**
Now simply bond those two saturated units together head to tail to make a four carbon backbone: $\text{-CH}_2\text{-CH(CH}_3\text{)-CH}_2\text{-CH(C}_6\text{H}_5\text{)-}$. Put a wavy or straight continuation bond at the left end and right end to show the chain goes on. That shows one molecule of each monomer incorporated.
Final answer: $\text{-CH}_2\text{-CH(CH}_3\text{)-CH}_2\text{-CH(C}_6\text{H}_5\text{)-}$ with continuation bonds through the backbone at both ends. Order of the two monomer units may be reversed.

hints: Look at the backbone of a polyalkenes such as poly(ethene), it contains only $\text{C-C}$ and $\text{C-H}$ single bonds.
walkthrough:
Explain inertness from polarity**
Picture the long saturated chain, just $\text{-CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{-}$ repeating. Carbon and hydrogen have very similar electronegativities, so $\text{C-C}$ and $\text{C-H}$ bonds have essentially no dipole. Water is a nucleophile that needs a partial positive carbon to attack, as in a $\text{C=O}$ or $\text{C-O}$ bond. With no polar site, water has nowhere to attack, so the chain cannot be hydrolysed and microbes cannot easily break it down.
Final answer: $\text{C-C}$ bonds in the backbone are non-polar with no dipole and cannot be attacked by water, so hydrolysis does not occur.

hints: Think of one chemical route that splits polar bonds in the chain, such as condensation polymers, using water with help.
Think of one physical route using light energy that can break $\text{C-C}$ bonds by radical formation even without water.
walkthrough:
Hydrolysis route**
Some polymers contain polar linkages like esters or amides. Warm aqueous acid or alkali, or natural enzymes secreted by microorganisms, can hydrolyse those linkages, cutting the long chain into small soluble monomers.

Light route**
High energy UV light can be absorbed by the polymer, breaking $\text{C-C}$ or $\text{C-H}$ bonds homolytically to form radicals. This photodegradation weakens and embrittles the plastic, breaking it into smaller fragments even when hydrolysis is not possible.

Final answer: 1. Hydrolysis by aqueous acid or alkali, or by enzymes.
2. Degradation by UV light (photodegradation).
